VA_COACH.WELCOME_P1: You are about to explore particle collisions in the ALICE detector.
VA_COACH.WELCOME_P2: Beams travel through the beam pipe, an ultra-high-vacuum tube, until they meet at the interaction point inside ALICE.
VA_COACH.WELCOME_P3: You will build the detector piece by piece, learning about the role and importance of every part of the detector. Ready?
VA_COACH.DONE_BODY: All detector parts are in place. Visibility and track options are in the right-hand panel. You can now start a short tutorial on how to use this exercise, or skip and explore on your own.
VA_COACH.DONE_BODY_WORKSHOP: All detector parts are in place. Visibility and track options are in the right-hand panel.

ITS.TITLE: ITS (Inner Tracking System)
ITS.BODY: The ITS is the innermost particle tracking detector, located closest to the point where protons or heavy ions collide. It is built from extremely thin silicon sensors that record the passage of charged particles with a precision of just a few micrometres - less than the thickness of a human hair. This allows physicists to determine the exact point where particles are produced and to detect particles that decay almost immediately after their creation, before they can reach the outer detectors.
ITS.B1: Determine the primary vertex with a resolution better than 100 micrometres
ITS.B2: Reconstruct secondary vertices needed for charm and hyperon decays
ITS.B4: Improve the momentum and angle resolution for particles reconstructed by the Time Projection Chamber (TPC)

FIT.TITLE: FIT (Fast Interaction Trigger)
FIT.BODY: The FIT is one of the first detectors to respond after a particle collision in the ALICE experiment. It is designed to detect collisions almost instantly and provide a precise timing signal that tells the rest of the experiment when an interaction has occurred. This early timing information is essential for triggering data acquisition and for synchronizing other detectors.
FIT.B1: Detect collisions in real time and trigger the data recording system.
FIT.B2: Measure the collision time with very high precision.
FIT.B3: Reject background events that are not true particle collisions.
FIT.B4: Support other detectors, such as TOF, by providing accurate timing information.

TPC.TITLE: TPC (Time Projection Chamber)
TPC.BODY: The TPC is the largest tracking detector in ALICE and one of the largest gas detectors ever built for particle physics. Charged particles ionize the gas as they pass through, leaving trails of free electrons that drift in an electric field to the readout chambers. From these signals, physicists reconstruct three-dimensional tracks with high precision, even when a single heavy-ion collision produces tens of thousands of particles. The TPC also helps identify particles by measuring how much energy they lose in the gas.
TPC.B1: Reconstruct particle tracks and visualize the paths of thousands of particles created in a single collision
TPC.B2: Identify different types of particles by measuring how they lose energy while passing through the gas
TPC.B3: Measure particle momentum, helping scientists understand their motion and interactions
TPC.B4: Study the properties of the quark-gluon plasma created in high-energy heavy-ion collisions

TRD.TITLE: TRD (Transition Radiation Detector)
TRD.BODY: The TRD is a detector designed mainly to identify electrons among the many different particles produced in high-energy collisions. It uses a phenomenon called transition radiation, which occurs when a very fast charged particle passes through the boundary between two different materials and emits X-ray radiation. Electrons produce this radiation much more efficiently than heavier particles, so the TRD can separate them from particles such as pions. That makes it important for studies involving electrons, including investigations of the quark-gluon plasma in heavy-ion collisions.
TRD.B1: Identify electrons and separate them from other types of particles.
TRD.B2: Study electron production in high-energy proton and heavy-ion collisions.
TRD.B3: Investigate the quark-gluon plasma and the extreme conditions created after collisions.
TRD.B4: Improve event reconstruction by providing additional information about detected particles.

TOF.TITLE: TOF (Time Of Flight)
TOF.BODY: The TOF detector measures how long particles take to travel from the collision point to the detector, with an accuracy of about 50 picoseconds (50 × 10<sup>−12</sup> s). Combining this travel time with the distance covered and the particle’s momentum gives its velocity, and from that its identity. In this way the TOF can distinguish pions, kaons, and protons even when they move at nearly the speed of light. Precise timing is especially useful because many particles produced in collisions have similar properties and need this extra handle for identification.
TOF.B1: Measure particle velocities with extremely high precision.
TOF.B2: Identify different types of particles by comparing their time of flight and momentum.
TOF.B3: Distinguish between pions, kaons, and protons produced in collisions.
TOF.B4: Improve the understanding of particle interactions in high-energy collisions.

PHOS.TITLE: PHOS (Photon Spectrometer)
PHOS.BODY: The PHOS is a high-resolution electromagnetic calorimeter built to measure the energy of photons and electrons as accurately as possible. Unlike the larger calorimeters, it focuses on precision rather than coverage. Dense scintillating crystals produce tiny flashes of light when particles pass through them, and from these flashes the particle energy can be determined very precisely. PHOS is especially useful for studying particles that decay into photons, such as pions.
PHOS.B1: Measure the energy of photons and electrons with very high precision.
PHOS.B2: Study particles that decay into photons, such as pions.
PHOS.B3: Investigate the quark-gluon plasma using electromagnetic probes.

L3.TITLE: L3 (Solenoid Magnet)
L3.BODY: The L3 magnet is the monumental solenoid around the ALICE detectors. It creates a strong magnetic field along the beam axis. Charged particles crossing this field have their paths bent by the Lorentz force. The bend direction shows the sign of the charge, and the curvature relates to momentum: higher-momentum particles bend less. Without the magnet, charged particles would fly in straight lines. With L3 on, their paths become the curved trajectories used to measure momentum.
L3.B1: Bend the paths of charged particles in a magnetic field.
L3.B2: Infer particle charge from the direction of track curvature.
L3.B3: Measure particle momentum from how strongly tracks bend.
L3.B4: Reveal the full curved event topology after the detector is assembled.

CALORIMETERS.TITLE: EMCal & DCal
CALORIMETERS.BODY: The electromagnetic calorimeters measure the energy of electrons and photons. When such a particle enters the detector, it creates an electromagnetic shower that deposits its energy inside the calorimeter and from this cascade physicists reconstruct the original particle’s energy. ALICE uses two sectors of the same technology, EMCal and DCal. Together they cover more of the detector, which is especially useful for studying jets and pairs of jets produced in opposite directions (di-jets).
CALORIMETERS.B1: Measure the energy of electrons and photons with high precision.
CALORIMETERS.B2: Study jets and back-to-back jet pairs (di-jets).
CALORIMETERS.B3: Investigate how particles lose energy while passing through the quark gluon plasma.

HOME.TITLE: Welcome to the ALICE Masterclass!
HOME.P1: The ALICE Collaboration has built a dedicated detector to exploit the unique physics potential of nucleus-nucleus collisions at LHC energies. Our aim is to study the physics of strongly interacting matter at the highest energy densities reached so far in the laboratory. In such conditions, an extreme phase of matter - called the quark-gluon plasma - is formed.
HOME.P2: Our universe is thought to have been in such a primordial state for the first few millionths of a second after the Big Bang. The properties of such a phase are key issues for Quantum Chromo Dynamics, the understanding of confinement-deconfinement and chiral phase transitions.
HOME.P3: For this purpose, we are carrying out a comprehensive study of the hadrons, electrons, muons and photons produced in the collisions of heavy nuclei. ALICE is also studying proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions both as a comparison with nucleus-nucleus collisions and in their own right.

INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.TITLE: Strange Particle Production
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.SUBTITLE: Exercise 1: Visual inspection
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.P1: The aim of the exercise is to search for strange particles produced from collisions at LHC and recorded by the ALICE experiment. Strange particles do not live long; they decay soon after their production. However, they live long enough to travel some distance (usually a few centimeters) from the interaction point (IP) from where they were produced (primary vertex). Their search is thus based on the identification of their decay products, which must originate from a common secondary vertex. Neutral strange particles, such as K0S, Λ and Λ̅, decay giving a characteristic decay pattern, called V0. The mother particle disappears some centimeters from the interaction point and two oppositely charged particles appear in its place, which are bent in opposite directions inside the magnetic field of the ALICE solenoid. In the following figures red tracks indicate positively charged particles, green tracks indicate negatively charged particles, and blue tracks indicate the bachelor pion in cascade decays. The decays we will be looking for are:
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.P2: We see that for a pion–pion final state the decay pattern is quasi-symmetric, whereas in the pion–proton final state the radius of curvature of the proton is larger than that of the pion: due to its higher mass, the proton carries most of the initial momentum.
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.P3: We will also be looking for cascade decays of charged strange particles. The Ξ− decays into π− and Λ; the Λ then decays into a proton and π−. Its antiparticle, the Ξ̅+, decays into π+ and Λ̅; the Λ̅ then decays into an antiproton and π+. In both cases the first pion is the bachelor (a single charged track) and is shown in blue. The search for V0s and cascades is based on the decay topology and the identification of the decay products; an additional confirmation of the particle identity is the calculation of its mass, based on the mass and momentum of the decay products.
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.P4: In this exercise, you will determine the number of strange particles in 15 pp collisions at a collision energy of 7 TeV. Particles can be identified through the topology of their decays. When you select tracks from a V0 or Cascade, the relevant numbers (momentum in the form (px,py,pz) and mass) will automatically be sent to the Calculator interface, and the invariant mass for the currently selected particles is calculated. Then you choose a particle type and click Add to include its mass in the graphs below.

VISUAL_ANALYSIS.EVENT_COMPLETE_BODY: You identified all particles - choose next event
VISUAL_ANALYSIS.ADD_HINT_SELECT_TYPE: Select a particle type before adding

HISTOGRAMS.TITLE: Histograms
HISTOGRAMS.INFO_BODY: A histogram shows how often values fall into chosen ranges. The horizontal axis shows those ranges (here: invariant mass), and the vertical axis shows how many observations fall in each one. The taller the bar, the more measurements landed in that range.

INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.TITLE: Strange Particle Production
INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.SUBTITLE: Exercise 2: Large Scale Analysis
INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.P1: The event display is a powerful tool which helps check the quality of the data and their reconstruction and gives a “feeling” of what events look like. However, in real life data analysis is not done visually — that would be far too tedious and time-consuming. To analyse the millions of events that we collect daily at the LHC we run programs, and this is what you will do here, in order to look for V0s in a bigger event sample.
INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.P2: You will now analyse recordings from hundreds of events at once. You can see that the invariant mass is a continuous distribution – this is because the pairs of pions combined are random, not coming from a common secondary vertex and can give any value of mass. Most of them are background.
INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.P3: In order to find the number of particles of a certain type, for example K0S, you need to find the number of events in the peak after background subtraction. In order to fit a curve (second degree polynomial) to the background, you first choose the fit range using the slider. To fit a Gaussian distribution to the signal you also have to select the range of the peak. When you click on Fit, the fitted functions are superimposed on the histogram and you can check visually whether the fit is reasonable. If you think the fitted functions match the data well, you can push the Accept button. For the background subtraction the coefficients of the second degree polynomial are used. After clicking the Accept button you will get, on the histogram, the total number of counts in the peak, the number of background counts and those which are signal.

INSTRUCTIONS_PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.TITLE: How tracks curve through ALICE
INSTRUCTIONS_PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.P1: Charged particles in ALICE travel through a strong magnetic field, and the Lorentz force pushes them sideways whenever their motion cuts across that field. Their tracks therefore curve: a stronger field or a lower momentum gives a tighter bend, while positive and negative charges curve opposite ways. Neutral particles feel no magnetic force, so they go straight. From how sharply a track bends, physicists can read the particle’s momentum.
INSTRUCTIONS_PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.P2: That field is shaped by a large solenoid around the barrel and a dipole near the muon detectors. Before the animation begins, the app follows every particle through this measured field and stores the paths. Once that is done, play and the time slider only reveal what was prepared, which keeps the motion smooth as you move through the event.
INSTRUCTIONS_PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.P3: Along the timeline you first see the protons approaching, then the collision, and finally the particles flying outward from the centre. If you change the field strength or reverse the solenoid, the bends should change with it; press Replay afterwards so the tracks are recalculated. Fading the detector layers or showing the field lines can make the same story easier to follow in the scene.

PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.WELCOME_TITLE: Particle Propagation in the Magnetic Field
PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.WELCOME_BODY_1: Two protons collide at the centre of ALICE. New particles fly outward, and the detector’s magnetic field bends the paths of those that carry electric charge.
PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.WELCOME_BODY_2: Press Start and the app prepares each trajectory through the real magnetic field of ALICE. Events with many particles may need a short moment to load.
PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.WELCOME_BODY_3: Afterwards, use the time slider to move from the approaching protons, through the collision, to the particles leaving the centre. Explore freely: the side panels let you change the field and look through the detector layers.

VA_TUTORIAL.WELCOME_P1: This short tutorial shows how to identify strange particles in a single ALICE collision and build invariant-mass histograms by hand.
VA_TUTORIAL.WELCOME_P2: You will turn on decay candidates, select daughter tracks that form a V, compare the calculated mass with known particle masses, then add each identification to the histograms.
VA_TUTORIAL.WELCOME_P3: You can skip anytime with ×. To start later, open Help with ? and choose Start tutorial.
VA_TUTORIAL.STEP_SCENE_BODY: Here you see a reconstructed proton-proton collision recorded by ALICE. This 3D view is the heart of the exercise: you search for strange-particle decays among the tracks and identify them one by one.
VA_TUTORIAL.STEP_VISIBILITY_BODY: Turn Decays on to highlight candidates for strange particles. They are found by an algorithm that looks for track pairs forming a letter V at a secondary vertex. You can turn Clusters off to make the event easier to read.
VA_TUTORIAL.STEP_DATASET_NAV_BODY: Use the dataset list to choose which sample to study, and the event buttons to move between collisions. These controls stay locked for this step of the tutorial so you can focus on one event first.
VA_TUTORIAL.STEP_CLICK_TRACKS_BODY: Find a V-shaped decay and click both daughter tracks: the red positive track and the green negative track. For a cascade, also click the blue bachelor. After both daughters are selected, the page scrolls to the Calculator and the tutorial continues.
VA_TUTORIAL.STEP_CALCULATOR_BODY: The Calculator shows the momentum components and masses of the tracks you selected. The Total value is the invariant mass of the mother particle. That is the main quantity you use to decide which strange particle you have found.
VA_TUTORIAL.STEP_IDENTIFY_BODY: Compare the Calculator total with the known masses in the Particles table, then choose the matching type. If you need help with decay shapes, click How to identify a particle?. Use Add to send the result to a histogram, or Undo to correct a mistake. Start tutorial stays disabled while this guide is open.
VA_TUTORIAL.STEP_HISTOGRAMS_BODY: Each accepted identification adds one entry to the matching invariant-mass histogram. After many events, real particles form peaks near their known masses, while random combinations stay as a smooth background. Use Bins to change how fine the mass intervals are.
VA_TUTORIAL.STEP_UPLOAD_BODY: When you are logged in, Upload data sends your identified particles to the teacher session so the class results can be collected. This is disabled for the Demo dataset.
VA_TUTORIAL.STEP_FINISH_BODY: When every decay track in this collision has been used, the particle selector is replaced by Next event. Press it to analyse the next collision and keep filling the histograms. Press Done to close the tutorial.

LSA_TUTORIAL.WELCOME_P1: The event display helps you build intuition about single events, but real LHC analysis uses programs over millions of events.
LSA_TUTORIAL.WELCOME_P2: Here you analyse hundreds of events at once by studying the invariant-mass distribution of V0 candidates and extracting signal yields with a fit.
LSA_TUTORIAL.WELCOME_P3: You can skip this tour anytime using the × button. To start it later, open the Help panel via the ? icon in the toolbar and click Start tutorial.
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_SETUP_BODY: Select the strange particle: the Kaon KS0, the Lambda Λ, or the Anti-Lambda Λ̄. Then choose the collision system: pp or Pb-Pb. For Pb-Pb also pick the centrality class - how head-on the nuclei collided. When ready, click Open histogram to load the spectrum. The tour advances automatically after loading.
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_SPECTRUM_BODY: This plot shows how often each invariant mass appears in your sample. The smooth broad shape is mostly random background from track pairs that do not come from the same decay. A real strange particle adds a narrow peak near its known mass. Your task is to measure that peak.
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_SIGNAL_BODY: Drag the Signal range so it covers the peak you want to fit. A Gaussian will model that peak. Keep the window wide enough for the peak, but avoid unrelated bumps. The coloured band on the histogram shows your choice.
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_BACKGROUND_BODY: Drag the Background range over a smooth region next to the peak. A 2nd-order polynomial fits that continuum and is later used under the peak. Watch the coloured band update as you drag.
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_FIT_BODY: Press Fit to draw the background polynomial and the signal Gaussian on the histogram.
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_CHECK_TITLE: Does the model match the data?
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_CHECK_BODY: Check that the polynomial follows the continuum away from the peak and that the Gaussian sits on top of the excess. Poor range choices show up as obvious mismatches. If it looks wrong, adjust the ranges and Fit again.
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_RESULT_ACTIONS_BODY: Accept saves the signal yield from your fit. Undo removes the last saved result. Clear fit removes the curves from the histogram so you can fit again, without deleting accepted rows.
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_RESULT_ACTIONS_BODY_WORKSHOP: Accept saves the signal yield from your fit. Clear fit removes the curves from the histogram so you can fit again, without deleting accepted rows.
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_ENHANCEMENT_PLOT_BODY: This chart shows strangeness enhancement versus the number of participating nucleons for each centrality class. Points appear as you accept fits for Kaon, Lambda and Anti-Lambda.
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_RESULTS_BODY: Each accepted fit adds a row with the particle type, collision, centrality when applicable, and the signal estimate. This mirrors how you would tabulate yields in a paper-style analysis workflow.
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_RESULTS_SUMMARY_BODY: For each centrality class this table gathers your accepted fits: the measured particle counts, the detector efficiency, and the yield - how many strange particles are produced per collision after corrections. The key number is enhancement: the yield divided by the same yield in proton-proton collisions. A value above 1 means strange particles are created more often in heavy-ion collisions than in simple proton-proton ones - that is strangeness enhancement.
LSA_TUTORIAL.STEP_UPLOAD_BODY: When logged in, Upload data sends your table to the server session (pooling class results). If the button is disabled, sign in from the main flow first.

PROBLEM.EMPTY: The workspace is empty. Nothing was analysed.
PROBLEM.RUN_FAILED: The data could not be loaded, so nothing was analysed.
PROBLEM.NOTHING_PLOTTED: Nothing is drawn: the pipeline computes a result but never plots it.
PROBLEM.MULT_WITHOUT_EVENTS: There are no events to histogram. Whose multiplicity would this count?
PROBLEM.NO_EVENTS: No events were recorded for centrality {{centrality}}.
PROBLEM.MULT_BEFORE_EVENTS: The multiplicity is filled before any events are taken.
PROBLEM.HIST_WITHOUT_TRACKS: There are no tracks to histogram. Whose momenta would this count?
PROBLEM.NO_TRACKS: No tracks were recorded for centrality {{centrality}}.
PROBLEM.TRACKS_NOT_HISTOGRAMMED: The tracks are never sorted into momentum bins, so there is no spectrum.
PROBLEM.HIST_BEFORE_TRACKS: The p<sub>T</sub> histogram is filled before any tracks are taken.
PROBLEM.CENTRALITY_MISMATCH: The events come from {{events}} but the tracks from {{tracks}}: those are different collisions.
PROBLEM.TWO_REFERENCES: The spectrum is divided by two different references. R<sub>AA</sub> uses pp, R<sub>CP</sub> uses the peripheral class. Pick one.
PROBLEM.PP_NEEDS_ALICE_BINNING: The pp reference is published in the ALICE bins; your histogram uses {{binning}} bins, so the two cannot be divided bin by bin.
PROBLEM.RCP_SELF_DIVISION: Dividing the peripheral class by itself gives 1 everywhere, by construction.
PROBLEM.NO_PERIPHERAL: The peripheral reference class is missing from the data.
PROBLEM.DUPLICATE_DIVISION: The same division ({{op}}) is applied twice, which scales the result away by that factor.
PROBLEM.NCOLL_UNKNOWN: The number of collisions is not known for centrality {{centrality}}.
PROBLEM.NCOLL_MISMATCH: You divided by the number of collisions of {{chosen}} but analysed the tracks of {{tracks}}: the result is off by the ratio of the two.
PROBLEM.MISSING_BIN_WIDTH: The counts were never divided by the bin width, so wide bins look fuller than narrow ones and the shape is not physical.
PROBLEM.MISSING_EVENTS: The yield was never divided by the number of events, so the result says how long the detector was running rather than what one collision produces.
PROBLEM.MISSING_NCOLL: The yield was never divided by the number of collisions, so a Pb–Pb collision is compared to a single proton–proton collision.
PROBLEM.NO_REFERENCE: Nothing was divided by a reference spectrum, so this is a yield, not a nuclear modification factor.
PROBLEM.RAA_NOT_A_RATIO: R<sub>AA</sub> cannot be plotted: the spectrum is still a yield, not a ratio.
PROBLEM.RCP_NOT_A_RATIO: R<sub>CP</sub> cannot be plotted: the spectrum is still a yield, not a ratio.
PROBLEM.RAA_NEEDS_PP: R<sub>AA</sub> is the ratio to proton–proton collisions; this result was divided by something else.
PROBLEM.RCP_NEEDS_PERIPHERAL: R<sub>CP</sub> is the ratio to the peripheral class; this result was divided by something else.
PROBLEM.PT_IS_A_RATIO: This is plotted as a spectrum, but it has already been divided by a reference. It is a ratio.
PROBLEM.EMPTY_BINS: {{count}} bin(s) received no tracks at all and are left out; at high p<sub>T</sub> particles are simply too rare.
PROBLEM.COUNT_WITHOUT_EVENTS: There is no event selection to count.
PROBLEM.FILL_WITHOUT_HIST: There is no empty histogram to fill. Create one first.
PROBLEM.MISSING_NEVT_VAR: N_evt was never counted, so the yield cannot be divided by the number of events.
PROBLEM.MISSING_NCOLL_VAR: The number of collisions was never looked up, so it cannot be divided by.
PROBLEM.CLONE_WITHOUT_SPECTRUM: There is no spectrum to clone.
PROBLEM.PERIPHERAL_WITHOUT_SPECTRUM: Build and normalise a spectrum before loading the peripheral reference.
PROBLEM.DIVIDE_WITHOUT_SPECTRUM: There is no spectrum to divide.
PROBLEM.PP_NOT_LOADED: The pp reference was never loaded.
PROBLEM.PERIPHERAL_NOT_LOADED: The peripheral spectrum was never loaded.
PROBLEM.FOR_EACH_EMPTY: For each has nothing to run inside.
PROBLEM.PLOT_WITHOUT_SPECTRUM: There is no spectrum to plot.
PROBLEM.READ_WITHOUT_SPECTRUM: There is no spectrum to read a value from.

SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.CLASSES_LOCKED: Plot a p<sub>T</sub> spectrum for a centrality class first. This table fills in once you have a result.
SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.RESULTS_EMPTY: Nothing collected yet. Plot R<sub>AA</sub> for a centrality class and its line appears here.
SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.RESULTS_NOTE: A highlighted value was read with a Read value at block. The rest come straight from the plotted points.
SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.FOOTER_MULTIPLICITY: One entry per collision. Central collisions produce far more particles than peripheral ones, which is how the centrality classes are defined.
SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.FOOTER_MULT_VS_CENTRALITY: Every event as one point. The centrality of a collision is read off its multiplicity, so this plot is the definition of the classes you select.
SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.FOOTER_PT_SPECTRUM: How many particles are produced at each transverse momentum. Steps where the bin width changes are bookkeeping, not physics. Dividing by the bin width removes them.
SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.FOOTER_PT_WITH_PP: Dashed: the published proton–proton spectrum. Same shape, different height. Dividing one by the other is exactly what R<sub>AA</sub> does.
SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.FOOTER_RAA: RAA = 1 would mean Pb–Pb behaves like a stack of independent pp collisions. Values below the line at high pT show energy lost by partons crossing the hot medium. That loss is called jet quenching.
SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.FOOTER_RCP: Central over peripheral. No pp measurement is needed. The suppression shows up the same way, evidence that it grows with the size of the medium.

INSTRUCTIONS_EVENT_EXPLORATION.TITLE: Event Exploration
INSTRUCTIONS_EVENT_EXPLORATION.P1: Use the event display to inspect pp and Pb–Pb collisions and measure charged-particle multiplicity.
INSTRUCTIONS_EVENT_EXPLORATION.STEP1: Browse the events in your dataset. The first event is a pp collision at 7 TeV with B = 0 T — for familiarisation only, do not count it.
INSTRUCTIONS_EVENT_EXPLORATION.STEP2: For the following 30 pp collisions at 2.76 TeV, inspect the tracks and note the multiplicity.
INSTRUCTIONS_EVENT_EXPLORATION.STEP3: The last three events are Pb–Pb (peripheral, semi-central, central). Use auto-counting for these high-multiplicity events.
INSTRUCTIONS_EVENT_EXPLORATION.STEP4: Compare yields and compute the integrated nuclear modification factor R<sub>AA</sub>.

INSTRUCTIONS_SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.TITLE: Spectrum Analysis
INSTRUCTIONS_SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.P1: Assemble the analysis out of blocks and compute R<sub>AA</sub> as a function of transverse momentum, using all ~40 000 Pb–Pb events and the published pp reference.
INSTRUCTIONS_SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.STEP1: Start with the events: take one centrality class and histogram its multiplicity. The number of entries is N<sub>evt</sub>.
INSTRUCTIONS_SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.STEP2: Take the tracks of the same class and fill a p<sub>T</sub> histogram in the ALICE bins.
INSTRUCTIONS_SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.STEP3: Normalise it: divide by the bin width, by the number of events, and by the number of collisions of that class. Leave one out and the result is wrong.
INSTRUCTIONS_SPECTRUM_ANALYSIS.STEP4: Divide by the pp reference to get R<sub>AA</sub>, repeat for several classes, and report your values at 5.5 and 10 GeV/c.
